title: Quality Control Testing
description: Quality control testing, routine inspection of products to confirm they meet specified parameters, is excluded from qualified research under IRC § 41.
summary: Quality control testing, for U.S. federal R&D tax credit purposes under IRC Sections 41, 174, and 174A, is the routine testing or inspection of materials or products to confirm that particular units conform to specified parameters. It is excluded from qualified research for taxpayers claiming the credit, unlike testing that evaluates whether a product's design is appropriate.

body.text: Quality control testing, for U.S. federal R&D tax credit purposes under IRC Sections 41, 174, and 174A, is the routine testing or inspection of materials or products to confirm that particular units conform to specified parameters. It is excluded from qualified research for taxpayers claiming the credit, unlike testing that evaluates whether a product's design is appropriate.

Distinguishing excluded Quality Control (QC) Testing from eligible Qualified Research Activities (QRAs) is one of the most consequential boundary lines in U.S. federal Research and Development (R&D) tax credit compliance under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 41. While engineering and product development teams frequently view validation, inspection, and testing as an integrated operational continuum, federal income tax law imposes a binary classification: testing undertaken to resolve technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design through a scientific process of experimentation qualifies for federal tax incentives, whereas testing conducted to verify whether particular units of materials or products conform to pre-established parameters or conducted after commercial production begins is categorically disqualified.

First, effective generally for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, Public Law 119-21 (enacted July 4, 2025, commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) added 26 U.S.C. § 174A for domestic research or experimental expenditures and amended 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) to require that qualified research expenditures be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under Section 174A rather than Section 174, which now governs 15-year amortization of foreign research or experimental expenditures (and previously governed domestic and foreign amortization after December 31, 2021, under Public Law 115-97). Second, across current Treasury Regulations, the quality control exclusion operates through dual regulatory provisions: under Section 174 regulations, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) excludes the ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7) defines quality control testing while carving out testing to determine whether a product design is appropriate (replacing pre-2014 designations § 1.174-2(a)(3) and (a)(4)), while under Section 41 regulations, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v) explicitly excludes routine or ordinary testing or inspections for quality control. Furthermore, the regulatory examples contrasting paint-spraying nozzle conformance testing against shredding-blade material trial-and-error experimentation are codified in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Examples 2 and 3, rather than § 1.41-4(c)(10). Third, in federal appellate precedent, the Fifth Circuit decided Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States (757 F.3d 400) in 2014 rather than 2012 (affirming the 2010 Northern District of Texas judgment at 691 F. Supp. 2d 688), and in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287, 7th Cir. 2023), the shipyard subsidiary was Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS) rather than "Cornwallis," the Seventh Circuit verbatim characterized the dry-dock raise-and-lower test as "less experimentation than it is a quality control test that establishes whether a customer's specifications have been met," and the appellate court rejected the Tax Court's categorical exclusion of direct support, direct supervision, and pilot model fabrication from the 80% experimentation numerator. Fourth, primary regulatory text confirms the commercial production readiness rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i)–(iv), the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)–(3), and the Internal Use Software (IUS) High Threshold of Innovation standard of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).
Statutory and Regulatory Architecture Governing Quality Control Testing
The Section 174A and Section 174 Gateway and the Quality Control Exclusion

Under the statutory structure of the federal research credit, eligibility under IRC Section 41 depends first on satisfying the underlying threshold test for research and experimental (R&E) expenditures. Under current federal law in force through late 2026, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A) defines "qualified research" as research "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A". Enacted on July 4, 2025, by Public Law 119-21 (Title VII, § 70302(a), 139 Stat. 193), 26 U.S.C. § 174A(a) permits taxpayers to deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. Alternatively, under 26 U.S.C. § 174A(c), taxpayers may elect to charge domestic R&E expenditures to a capital account and amortize them ratably over a period of not less than 60 months beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures. In addition, Section 70302(e) and (f) of Public Law 119-21 (implemented via Revenue Procedure 2025-28) establishes two transition mechanisms: eligible small businesses meeting the gross receipts test of IRC § 448(c) may elect within one year of enactment to apply Section 174A retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, via amended returns, and taxpayers may utilize transition options to recover remaining unamortized domestic R&E amounts capitalized during taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025, including deducting such remaining unamortized amounts ratably over the two-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024.

Conversely, 26 U.S.C. § 174—which had been retitled "Amortization of research and experimental expenditures" by Public Law 115-97 (§ 13206) for amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021—was amended by Public Law 119-21 to apply to foreign research or experimental expenditures, which must be charged to capital account and amortized ratably over a 15-year period (with special disposition rules under § 70302(b)(1)(C)(ii) applying to property disposed, retired, or abandoned after May 12, 2025). Consequently, treating Section 174 alone as the current domestic deduction gateway is outdated for post-2024 taxable years and overlooks the capitalization regime that governed domestic research between 2022 and 2024.

Although Congress bifurcated the statutory deduction provisions between Section 174A (domestic) and Section 174 (foreign) in 2025, the substantive regulatory definition of "research or experimental expenditures" in 26 CFR § 1.174-2 continues to govern pre-2025 litigation and defines the qualitative boundary between experimental research and excluded quality control testing. Specifically, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1) provides that expenditures represent research and development costs in the "experimental or laboratory sense" if they are incurred for activities "intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product". Under § 1.174-2(a)(1), uncertainty exists "if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product or the appropriate design of the product". Crucially, the regulation as amended by Treasury Decision (T.D.) 9680 (effective for taxable years ending on or after July 21, 2014) clarifies that eligibility depends on the nature of the activity rather than the nature of the product or the level of technological advancement, that the ultimate success, failure, sale, or use of the product is not relevant to eligibility under Section 174, and that costs "may be eligible under section 174 if paid or incurred after production begins but before uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the product is eliminated". Conversely, under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(2) (Production costs), except as provided in the component shrinking-back rule of paragraph (a)(5), costs paid or incurred in the production of a product after the elimination of uncertainty concerning its development or improvement are not eligible under Section 174.

In T.D. 9680 (2014-32 I.R.B.), the Treasury Department added new paragraphs (a)(2), (a)(4), and (a)(5) to 26 CFR § 1.174-2 and redesignated former paragraphs (a)(3) through (a)(6) as paragraphs (a)(6) through (a)(9). Thus, across current Title 26 regulations, the quality control exclusion and its definitional boundary are codified across three specific provisions:

First, under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) (Research or experimental expenditures—exclusions), the regulation states that the term research or experimental expenditures does not include expenditures for "(i) The ordinary testing or inspection of materials or products for quality control (quality control testing)". Second, 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7) (Quality control testing) defines the exclusion and establishes an explicit carve-out protecting design verification: "For purposes of paragraph (a)(6)(i) of this section, testing or inspection to determine whether particular units of materials or products conform to specified parameters is quality control testing. However, quality control testing does not include testing to determine if the design of the product is appropriate." Third, under the Section 41 regulations, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v) (Surveys, studies, research relating to management functions, etc.) implements the statutory exclusion under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4) by providing that qualified research does not include activities relating to "(v) Routine or ordinary testing or inspections for quality control" (alongside efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, and routine data collections in § 1.41-4(c)(5)(i)–(iv)).

Treasury Regulations under both Section 174 and Section 41 provide concrete regulatory examples illustrating how this divide operates in practice. In 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 3 (Pilot model) and Example 4 (Product component redesign) trace the transition between pilot model experimentation, commercial production, quality control failure, and design reconfiguration. In Example 3, custom machine manufacturer U contracts to design and produce a custom machine to meet a customer's specifications. Because U has never designed a machine with those specifications and is uncertain whether the desired features can be integrated into a functional machine, U incurs a total of $31,000 on the project: $10,000 of costs on materials and labor to produce a pilot model (defined in § 1.174-2(a)(4) as any representation or model of a product produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty during development or improvement) and $1,000 for testing/engineering qualify under Section 174, whereas $20,000 incurred to produce the machine for sale to the customer based on the appropriate design is disallowed under § 1.174-2(a)(2) as a production cost. Building directly on Example 3, Example 4 (Product component redesign) assumes the same facts except that during a quality control test of the machine, a component fails to function due to the component's inappropriate design, causing U to incur an additional $8,000 (including design retesting) to reconfigure the component's design. Confirming the design-appropriateness carve-out of § 1.174-2(a)(7), Example 4 concludes that the $8,000 of costs represents research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense and therefore qualifies under Section 174. Similarly, Example 5 (Multiple pilot models) confirms that where manufacturer V incurs $5,000 to produce multiple models of a new product to test the appropriate design across extreme conditions (such as heat, cold, submersion, and vibration) before mass production, the entire $5,000 qualifies under Section 174 even if multiple models are tested in the same environment or subsequently sold to customers.

The paint-spraying nozzle and shredding-blade examples exist verbatim in the Section 41 regulations, but they are codified in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Examples 2 and 3 (illustrating the process of experimentation test), whereas 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 1 illustrates quality control testing and post-production exclusions in tire manufacturing.

In 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 2 (Routine Nozzle Verification Excluded as Quality Control), following Example 1 (where widget manufacturer X changes widget paint from blue to green for purely cosmetic reasons excluded under § 41(d)(3)(B)), X determines it must modify its painting process to accommodate the green paint's physical characteristics. X obtains detailed data from its paint supplier and consults the manufacturer of its paint-spraying machines, which informs X that it must acquire a new nozzle that operates with the green paint. X tests the nozzles to ensure that they work as specified by the manufacturer of the paint-spraying machines. The regulation holds that although modifying the painting process is a separate business component under § 41(d)(2)(A), X did not conduct a process of evaluating alternatives to eliminate uncertainty (because the machine manufacturer eliminated X's uncertainty), and "X's activities to test the nozzles to determine if the nozzles work as specified by the manufacturer of the paint spraying machines are in the nature of routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control."

By contrast, in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3 (Systematic Trial-and-Error Shredding Blade Testing Qualified), food manufacturer X seeks to modify its current production line to manufacture both a large-shred and a fine-shred version of a food product. A smaller, thinner shredding blade capable of producing a fine-shred version is not commercially available, and the material used in X's existing blade breaks when machined into smaller, thinner blades. Uncertain concerning the design of the new blade, "X engages in a systematic trial and error process of analyzing various blade designs and materials to determine whether the new shredding blade must be constructed of a different material from that of its existing shredding blade and, if so, what material will best meet X's functional requirements." The regulation concludes that X's activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation and satisfy the requirements of qualified research.

Complementing those examples, in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 1 (Production Belt Testing Excluded as Post-Production and Quality Control), tire manufacturer X develops a new tire material that retains heat longer and adheres to manufacturing equipment during tread cooling. X evaluates numerous options and conducts sophisticated tests on options for a new type of cooling belt (activities that may constitute qualified research). X then manufactures a set of belts for its production equipment, installs the belts, and tests the belts to make sure they were manufactured correctly. The regulation concludes that X's expenses to manufacture, install, and test the production belts were incurred after the belts met the taxpayer's functional and economic requirements (excluded as research after commercial production under § 41(d)(4)(A) and § 1.41-4(c)(2)), and further states that "testing or inspection to determine whether the production belts were manufactured correctly is quality control testing under § 1.174-2(a)(4) [redesignated as § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and (a)(7)] and thus is not qualified research under section 41(d)(1)(A) and paragraph (a)(2)(i) of this section."
Research After Commercial Production Under Section 41(d)(4)(A)

Even if a testing or validation activity is not classified as ordinary quality control inspection under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) or § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v), it must clear the statutory time-boundary exclusion for post-production activities. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), the term "qualified research" excludes: "Research after commercial production. Any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component."

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i), "Activities are conducted after the beginning of commercial production of a business component if such activities are conducted after the component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for the component's sale or use." IRS examination guidance notes that examiners look for formal "product release" sign-off documents where responsible managers certify that a new product or production method is released for production. Furthermore, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii) (Certain additional activities related to the business component), the following six activities are per se deemed to occur after the beginning of commercial production of a business component:

items: Preproduction planning for a finished business component (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(A));
Trouble shooting involving detecting faults in production equipment or processes (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(D));
Accumulating data relating to production processes (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(E)); and
Debugging flaws in a business component (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(F)).

body.text: As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide emphasizes, this per se list includes "debugging" activities, but does not exclude the "correction of flaws" where fundamental design defects require engineering reconfiguration (as illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 4). Furthermore, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) (Activities related to production process or technique) establishes a vital bifurcation rule: in cases involving the development of both a product and a manufacturing or other commercial production process for that product, the commercial production exclusion applies separately for the activities relating to the development of the product and the activities relating to the development of the process. Specifically, "even after a product meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements, activities relating to the development of the manufacturing process still may constitute qualified research, provided that the development of the process itself separately satisfies the requirements of section 41(d) and this section, and the activities are conducted before the process meets the taxpayer's basic functional and economic requirements or is ready for commercial use." In the pharmaceutical context, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv) (Clinical testing) further provides that clinical testing of a pharmaceutical product prior to its commercial production in the United States is not treated as occurring after the beginning of commercial production even if the product is commercially available in other countries, and that additional clinical testing conducted after Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for a specific therapeutic use and commercial readiness is not treated as occurring after commercial production if undertaken to establish new functional uses, characteristics, indications, combinations, dosages, or delivery forms that must be approved by the FDA.

In software development, the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software likewise state that "Quality assurance (QA)/Testing (module, systems, integration, alpha, beta, performance, stress, regression, user acceptance, and manual testing, etc.) occurs throughout the development and maintenance processes," noting that beta and subsequent testing are typically performed against the entire software business component rather than just the modified portion, and requiring examiners to separate development experimentation from post-development maintenance debugging and routine QA.
The Four-Part Test and Intersecting Exclusions

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2), research activities related to the development or improvement of a business component constitute qualified research only if they satisfy four cumulative statutory tests: (1) the Section 174A (formerly Section 174) Expenditure Test under § 41(d)(1)(A), requiring that expenditures qualify as domestic research or experimental expenditures under 26 U.S.C. § 174A and 26 CFR § 1.174-2; (2) the Discovering Technological Information Test under § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), requiring that research be undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature (fundamentally relying on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4)) and intended to eliminate uncertainty concerning capability, method, or appropriate design under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i); (3) the Business Component Test under § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and (d)(2), requiring that the taxpayer intend the discovered information to be useful in developing a new or improved product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business, applied separately to each discrete component and plant process under § 41(d)(2)(A)–(C); and (4) the Process of Experimentation and "Substantially All" Test under § 41(d)(1)(C) and (d)(3), requiring that substantially all (80% or more under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6)) of the research activities with respect to the business component constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality.

Although routine quality control testing frequently utilizes principles of engineering, metallurgy, chemistry, or computer science—and relates to an identifiable business component—it typically fails both the Uncertainty Test and the Process of Experimentation Test. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(i), uncertainty exists only if "the information available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the business component, or the appropriate design of the business component". As the Seventh Circuit underscored in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), generic manufacturing or construction uncertainty—questions such as whether a tire fits, what screws attach a panel, whether a weld holds a truss, or whether an assembled vessel meets a customer's contractual deadweight or submersion parameters—is inherent in all physical production and does not satisfy Section 174 or Section 41. Quality control testing asks whether a particular manufactured unit conforms to an already-established design parameter (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7)), whereas qualified research testing asks whether the underlying design itself is appropriate and capable of achieving the functional result.

Furthermore, under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a "process of experimentation" must be "a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities". Relying fundamentally on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science, it "must be an evaluative process and generally should be capable of evaluating more than one alternative" through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial-and-error methodology. Crucially, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) contains an explicit anti-bootstrapping provision: "Uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of the business component (e.g., its appropriate design) does not establish that all activities undertaken to achieve that new or improved business component constitute a process of experimentation." At the same time, 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) confirms that a taxpayer need not seek information that "exceeds, expands or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in the particular field of science or engineering" and need not succeed in developing the component (supplemented by the patent safe harbor of § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii) for utility patents issued under 35 U.S.C. § 151). However, deploying advanced scientific instrumentation does not elevate routine conformance verification into a process of experimentation if the test merely checks adherence to known parameters.

Three additional statutory exclusions under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3) and (d)(4) frequently intersect with quality control and validation testing. First, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(3) (Adaptation of existing business components) exclude activities relating to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need (illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Examples 3–7), though the exclusion does not apply merely because a business component is intended for a specific customer. In a hypothetical illustration, testing an existing electric motor adapted to operate on a foreign client's standard voltage to verify that it runs properly constitutes excluded adaptation and quality control verification unless the adaptation entailed resolving design uncertainty through systematic experimentation. Second, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) (Duplication of existing business component) exclude activities relating to reproducing an existing business component, in whole or in part, from a physical examination of the component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information (illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 8). While 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(4) clarifies that this exclusion "does not apply merely because the taxpayer examines an existing business component in the course of developing its own business component," testing a reproduced component merely to confirm that it matches a competitor's specifications is excluded duplication and conformance inspection. Third, 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii) categorically bar any research activity or testing relating to "style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors," such as the customer color-preference testing in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 12.
Experimental Iteration Versus Routine Verification

The conceptual boundary separating qualified experimental testing from excluded quality control testing is framed as an iterative scientific loop versus a linear disposition check. In Tax Court precedent established in Union Carbide Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2009-50) and affirmed by the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287), the courts held that a process of experimentation requires adherence to the scientific method: "a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense". Under this standard, qualified research testing begins with a technical hypothesis regarding an uncertain design variable (illustrated in a hypothetical example by whether a novel flange design can withstand 5,000 PSI of pressure), subjects a prototype to trial, analyzes the failure data (such as rupture at 4,200 PSI), refines the hypothesis by reconfiguring the geometry or material, and retests the modified design until the technical uncertainty is resolved.

By contrast, routine quality control testing operates along a linear conformance path (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7)). The design parameter is already fixed before the test begins (illustrated in a hypothetical example by a production specification that a machined part measure 10 mm ± 0.1 mm). The inspector measures the unit against that fixed specification to drive an immediate operational disposition—ship, rework, or scrap—without altering the underlying engineering design (unless a failure reveals that the component design itself is inappropriate, triggering experimental reconfiguration and design retesting as illustrated in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 4).

Moreover, depicting expense eligibility as an automatic 100% pre-production plateau followed by an absolute 0% post-production cliff oversimplifies three governing legal doctrines under Title 26, as detailed in the comparative table below:

cells: Assumes 100% expense eligibility across Concept, Design, Prototyping, and Validation Testing phases.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), a business component qualifies only if 80% or more ("substantially all") of its research activities, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis, constitute elements of a process of experimentation. Even if a component passes the 80% threshold, non-qualifying activities (such as ordinary QC inspection under § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i)) remain excluded from QREs, and if non-experimental testing exceeds 20% of total research activities, the entire component fails unless narrowed via the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2).
Direct Support, Direct Supervision, and Pilot Model Fabrication
Visually separates prototyping and validation testing from production without specifying how support labor and pilot model construction enter the 80% fraction.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii), 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4), and the Seventh Circuit's holding in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287, 2023), pilot model fabrication costs incurred prior to eliminating design uncertainty, as well as direct supervision and direct support of experimental research, are eligible to be included in both the numerator and the denominator of the 80% "substantially all" fraction when directed at resolving technical uncertainty through a process of experimentation.
Depicts an absolute, permanent drop to 0% eligibility once Commercial Production of the product begins.

While product-level research terminates once the product meets basic functional and economic requirements (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A); 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i)), three exceptions apply: (1) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), and Union Carbide (T.C. Memo. 2009-50), manufacturing process research constitutes a separate business component that can qualify after commercial product sales begin (though ordinary raw-material supplies incorporated into goods sold to customers are disallowed under 697 F.3d 104); (2) under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5) and (a)(11) Example 4, component redesign and design retesting triggered when a QC test reveals an inappropriate design qualify under Section 174/174A; and (3) under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv), post-approval clinical trials for new FDA-approved indications remain eligible.

body.text: Judicial Precedent Defining Testing and Quality Control Boundaries

Federal appellate and U.S. Tax Court decisions over the past fifteen years have rigorously policed the boundary between experimental validation and routine quality control, establishing strict evidentiary burdens for taxpayers claiming testing wages, prototype fabrication costs, and trial-run supplies.
Little Sandy Coal Company, Inc. v. Commissioner

In Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. March 7, 2023), affirming T.C. Memo. 2021-15 (121 T.C.M. (CCH) 1113), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit addressed research credit claims by a taxpayer whose shipbuilding subsidiary, Corn Island Shipyard, Inc. (CIS), designed and built 11 first-in-class custom vessels. At trial, the parties litigated two representative projects: Project 720, the Apex 720 Tanker (a tanker barge involving modifications to a prior design), and Project 730, the Detyens Dry Dock (a floating dry dock built for client Detyens).

To substantiate its process of experimentation on the Detyens Dry Dock, the taxpayer pointed to a partial "raise-and-lower" submersion test conducted by CIS after constructing the vessel, as well as deadweight surveys conducted on the Tanker:

"The tax court found that CIS's partial raise-and-lower test for the Dry Dock did not establish that the design of every element of the vessel remained uncertain, and thus constituted a process of experimentation. This raise-and-lower test, too, is less experimentation than it is a quality control test that establishes whether a customer's specifications have been met. § 1.174-2(a)(7). It merely ascertains whether a dry dock submerges and rises as designed and according to a customer's desired parameters. In fact, the client, Detyens—not CIS—conducted a full raise-and-lower test after taking delivery of the vessel at its shipyard."

Applying 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and (a)(7), the Seventh Circuit held that both the dry-dock raise-and-lower test and the tanker deadweight surveys were non-qualifying quality control tests conducted to verify conformance with customer parameters rather than experimental procedures designed to resolve uncertainty regarding the appropriate design of the vessels.

In the underlying Tax Court opinion (T.C. Memo. 2021-15), the Tax Court had held that direct supervision, direct support, and wages incurred to fabricate a pilot model (under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4)) must be included in the denominator of the 80% "substantially all" fraction under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) but could never be included in the numerator because physical fabrication and support were not per se experimentation or testing. The Seventh Circuit explicitly rejected the Tax Court's narrow construction of the numerator, stating: "We disagree with some aspects of the tax court's reasoning, but ultimately, Taxpayer claimed more tax credit than it could prove." Specifically, the Seventh Circuit held that "the numerator is broad enough to encompass research activities that are not per se experimentation or testing," reasoning that "If a pilot model, by definition, is produced to resolve the correct type of uncertainty, it would be odd that pilot model production activities should not constitute research activities deductible under section 174," and confirming that direct supervision, direct support, and pilot model construction costs can enter the numerator when the pilot model is used in a methodical plan to evaluate alternatives and resolve design uncertainty.

Despite winning this legal point on the composition of the fraction, the taxpayer lost the appeal entirely because it pursued an "all or nothing" whole-vessel strategy ("by choosing an 'all or nothing' strategy, Taxpayer swung for the fences and missed"), relied on generalized assertions of vessel novelty ("the novelty of a business component is not a proper heuristic for the substantially all test"), ignored the principle that "a manufacturer may not simply 'add a few new bells and whistles' on a pre-existing product and claim uncertainty as to the whole," and relied on arbitrary employee time estimates. As the Seventh Circuit concluded, the taxpayer "did not offer a principled way to determine what portion of the employee activities for each vessel constituted elements of a process of experimentation, much less research activities," admonishing future claimants that "other taxpayers seeking to avail themselves of the research tax credit would be well advised to document research activities for subcomponents" under the shrinking-back rule.
Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States

In Trinity Industries, Inc. v. United States, 691 F. Supp. 2d 688 (N.D. Tex. 2010), aff'd, 757 F.3d 400 (5th Cir. 2014), the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit evaluated research tax credit claims by shipbuilder Trinity Industries for first-in-class vessels that Trinity characterized as full-scale "prototypes".

In Phase I of the bench trial, the district court evaluated six vessel development projects claimed on an "all-or-nothing" whole-vessel basis under the four-part test of IRC § 41(d). Two vessels satisfied all four requirements of IRC § 41(d) at the whole-vessel level: the Mark V Special Operations Craft (a high-speed military craft with demanding speed, stealth, transport, and operational requirements) and the Dirty Oil Barge. The remaining four Phase I vessels failed the fourth requirement—that 80% or more of total research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation—and were disallowed in full: the Extra Fast Patrol Boat (XFPB) (which possessed some experimental features but was found "fairly routine" overall), the T-AGS 60 Oceanographic Survey Ship (a sophisticated oceanographic research vessel that contained some innovations but failed the overall 80% threshold), the Crew Rescue Boat (disallowed because it was not a technologically complex boat to build), and the Hurley Dredge (disallowed because Trinity constructed the vessel based on a design provided to Trinity by a third party). In Phase II of the trial, the court evaluated two additional vessel projects, holding that the Queen of New Orleans qualified for tax credits while the Penn Tugs project failed the process-of-experimentation test.

The Fifth Circuit opinion explains that for an entire vessel project to qualify as a prototype, the identification, configuration, and integration of the components had to be sufficiently complex and at least 80% of total development activities had to consist of a process of experimentation (such as computer modeling, testing, and retesting across at least four design revisions to assess structural integrity under wave action on the Penn Tugs), without using the phrase "tested to destruction". Regarding the shrinking-back rule (26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)), the Fifth Circuit explicitly noted that the rule allows a taxpayer to demonstrate that smaller subcomponents of an overall project satisfy the process-of-experimentation requirement even if the project as a whole fails—giving the specific illustrative example of "proving that the development of a vessel's engine was sufficiently experimental even if the entire ship was not". Because Trinity took an "all-or-nothing" approach on its amended tax returns and did not offer proof of claim-year expenses at the subcomponent level—partly because Hurricane Katrina destroyed many of its financial records—the court evaluated each project as a whole and could not apply the shrinking-back rule to isolate qualifying subcomponents on the T-AGS 60 or XFPB.
Union Carbide Corp. v. Commissioner

In Union Carbide Corp. & Subs. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50, 97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207 (March 10, 2009), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Tax Court (Judge Goeke) and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit established foundational precedent governing plant-scale production trials, the separation of process versus product business components, the line between validation and experimentation, and the disallowance of raw-material supplies incorporated into commercial goods sold to customers.

Union Carbide Corporation (UCC) claimed research tax credits for plant-scale experimental runs conducted on full-sized commercial chemical reactors during production operations, litigating five sample projects before the Tax Court, three of which are central to testing and quality control analysis. First, in the Amoco Anticoking Project, UCC regularly had to suspend operation of its ethylene manufacturing furnaces at its Taft hydrocarbons unit to remove "coke," a brittle carbon byproduct that impeded ethylene production. UCC evaluated an anticoking chemical pretreatment technology (pretreating furnace coils twice) to reduce coke buildup and extend furnace run times. Applying 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C) and the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), the Tax Court held that the activities relating primarily to testing the Amoco anticoking technology constituted qualified research on a separate manufacturing process business component even though ethylene was already a commercial product. Second, in the UCAT-J Catalyst Project, conducted in Reactor 2 at UCC's Star facility, UCC tested a high-productivity catalyst system (UCAT-J) to reduce polyethylene manufacturing costs across multiple experimental production runs (including Run 3, Run 7 on DJM-1725H, Run 15 on DJM-1732H, and Run 16 on DJM-1725H). To control resin stickiness, film appearance gels, and triethylaluminum (TEAl) starvation, UCC's Process R&D team recommended lowering ethylene partial pressure below 90 psi—an experimental step never before attempted at Star with UCAT-J that carried risks of decreased catalyst productivity, lower resin average particle size, increased fines, and reactor fouling—and implemented periodic TEAl shots. The Tax Court held that the UCAT-J process trials satisfied the process-of-experimentation requirement. Third, in the Sodium Borohydride Project (and the Olefins-1 one-hole spuds project), the Tax Court disallowed the claimed research: in the Sodium Borohydride project, UCC failed the process-of-experimentation test because it did not analyze data beyond establishing that injecting sodium borohydride into crude butadiene reduced acetaldehyde impurities below 100 parts per million (ppm)—meaning UCC was merely validating results rather than experimenting with optimal dosages or injection rates—while on Olefins-1, objective information available to UCC from past experience and vendor John Zink Co. eliminated uncertainty at the outset.

On the critical question of supply QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and § 41(b)(2)(C), UCC claimed the costs of raw materials (such as ethylene feedstock, fuel gas, and base resin inputs totaling 743,987 pounds of aim-grade resin in UCAT-J Run 3 and 737,200 pounds of aim-grade plus 137,100 pounds of off-grade resin in UCAT-J Run 7 and a November 1994 run) consumed during the Amoco Anticoking and UCAT-J plant runs. Both the Tax Court and the Second Circuit (697 F.3d 104) disallowed those raw-material supply costs in full. Referencing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1) (which excludes "indirect research expenditures") and pre-renumbering Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4) on quality control, the courts held that because "research was conducted on products that were in the process of being manufactured for sale and were in fact sold," raw-material supply costs that the taxpayer would have incurred regardless of the research are ineligible inventory/COGS costs rather than "supplies used in the conduct of qualified research". Deferring to the IRS's interpretation under Auer v. Robbins (and Chevron principles that academic commentary notes taxpayers have begun challenging following Loper Bright), the Second Circuit held that only additional or incremental supplies purchased specifically to conduct the research qualify for the credit. (The exact judicial standard under Union Carbide is whether the supplies are incremental research supplies rather than raw materials incorporated into commercial goods manufactured for sale.)
Suder v. Commissioner

In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201, 108 T.C.M. 355 (decided October 1, 2014, by Judge Vasquez), the U.S. Tax Court examined research tax credit claims across 76 hardware and software product development projects (with 12 representative projects stipulated for trial: Arcadia, Chameleon, Clark Kent, Rio Grande, Mad Max, Express FSII, Suzuki, Phoenix, Pony, DLC0, DLC82, and IVC1212) conducted between 2004 and 2007 by Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI), a Subchapter S corporation owned 90% by CEO Eric Suder and 10% by COO Douglas Boyd that designed telephone systems for small and midsize businesses. Employing roughly 125 employees (including 40 engineers) and generating approximately $38.5 million in gross revenues, ESI had achieved ISO-9000 certification in 2000 and followed a standardized, multi-step development process progressing from Concept → Hardware → Software → Testing.

The IRS disallowed ESI's claimed credits in full, contending that ESI's projects were "routine engineering," "ordering off a menu," or "repackaging and rearranging of earlier designs" that faced only normal scheduling or resource uncertainties, and arguing further that research activities ended before customer beta testing. Rejecting the IRS's position, the Tax Court held that 11 of the 12 representative projects qualified as research activities under Section 41(d), stating that "Neither section 41 nor the regulations thereunder require taxpayers to 'reinvent the wheel'" and confirming that relying on established engineering principles or ISO-9000 standards does not disqualify research from constituting a five-step scientific process of experimentation (conceptually hypothesizing technical alternatives, testing alternatives in a scientific manner, analyzing results, refining or discarding hypotheses, and repeating the process as necessary).

On the specific boundary between experimental testing and quality control, Suder established three critical holdings. First, regarding product assurance lab testing and iterative bug fixing, after contractors Alta Via (Gerber files) and GTECH manufactured roughly 20 physical prototypes per project, ESI's product assurance lab tested the prototypes, generated bug reports, and prioritized issues; ESI's engineers reproduced the bugs, fixed them by priority, or—in cases of serious bugs—completely redesigned the prototype before resubmitting it for retesting. The court held that this documented record of bug reports, release notes, schematics, and testing logs evidenced a systematic process of experimentation. Second, regarding internal alpha testing and external beta testing, ESI's engineering department installed prototypes into ESI's own business phone system for internal alpha testing, during which CEO Suder personally "touched, played with, and blessed" every prototype. During external beta testing—the final testing stage before commercial release—ESI worked through resellers to recruit 20 to 25 business customers per product, providing prototype devices at a discount in exchange for real-world usage and performance feedback. Rejecting the IRS's argument that beta testing is post-research validation, the Tax Court held that because design uncertainties persisted and "ESI's engineers continued to fix bugs in the product during the beta testing process," beta testing was a necessary, qualified step in the process of experimentation. Third, regarding differentiated wage allocations between engineering and QC personnel, Senior VP of Product Development Harvey Wende compiled yearly allocation spreadsheets that allocated 100% for engineers, product managers, CTO Buzz Hansen, and himself, 75% for CEO Suder (conservatively reduced from 80% to avoid the "substantially all" rule), 25% for COO Boyd, and only 5% to 10% for Quality Control (QC), shipping, and routine test technician personnel.

Two important limitations accompany Suder's holding. First, although the Tax Court accepted SVP Wende's credible testimony to establish wage nexus under Cohan v. Commissioner and United States v. McFerrin without project-by-project time tracking, the court held under 26 U.S.C. § 174(e) that a substantial portion of CEO Suder's $8.7 million to $11 million annual compensation (which accounted for two-thirds of ESI's claimed wage QREs) was unreasonable, accepting the IRS expert report and ruling that only approximately 20% of the compensation paid to Suder constituted reasonable compensation eligible for QRE treatment. Second, in the October 4, 2016 Treasury and IRS final regulations preamble (Credit for Increasing Research Activities, 2016-23174), the government explicitly clarified that Suder is not inconsistent with Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10), Example 9 because in Suder the Tax Court "did not address whether 'routine programming' could meet the process of experimentation requirement."
Industry and Software Testing Applications
Manufacturing, Engineering, and Laboratory Testing

Across industrial manufacturing, chemical processing, pharmaceutical development, and hardware engineering, whether a testing protocol qualifies under IRC Section 41 and Section 174A or fails as excluded quality control turns on the objective purpose and timing of the test under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and (a)(7). While an R&D tax credit vendor overview (onshore.com) highlights prototyping, first articles, CNC programming/machining, defect reduction, and process scale-up/validation as common manufacturing claim areas, authoritative IRS examination guides enforce rigorous boundaries separating experimental discovery from routine shop-floor or laboratory inspection.

Specifically, in IRS Publication 5931 (Pharmaceutical Industry Research Credit Audit Technique Guide, Rev. April 2024), the IRS categorizes quality control, equipment calibration, and qualification protocols across all four stages of drug development as "High Risk Activities"—defined in IRS examination guidelines as activities that usually fail to constitute qualified research under IRC § 41(d). In the Discovery and Development Stage, Publication 5931 designates as High Risk: (1) "Quality control and/or inspection of raw materials in the clinical laboratory," (2) "Preventative maintenance, calibration, and inspection of laboratory equipment," and (3) "Equipment qualification (Installation Qualification (IQ), Operational Qualification (OQ), and Performance Qualification (PQ))". Similarly, it designates as High Risk "Quality control/inspection of drug for use in animal testing" in the Pre-Clinical Research Stage, "Quality control and/or inspection of drug for use in human clinical trials" in the Clinical Research Stage, and "Quality control/inspection of commercial drug for distribution" in the FDA Post-Market Safety Monitoring Stage. This administrative guidance reinforces 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(11), Example 4 and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 2: inspecting incoming raw materials, calibrating laboratory instruments, executing standard IQ/OQ/PQ equipment checks to confirm that machinery operates within vendor specifications, or inspecting batches for clinical or commercial release are excluded quality control activities unless a failure exposes an inappropriate product or process design and triggers systematic engineering reconfiguration and design retesting.

In Plastic Injection Molding, when a molder develops a new micro-molded component with tight tolerances where material shrinkage and warpage are uncertain, conducting "Scientific Molding" or "Decoupled Molding" rheology trials—systematically varying melt temperature, injection velocity, hold pressure, and cooling time across short-shot trials and performing destructive optical and mechanical stress tests on trial parts to establish the viable manufacturing process window—aligns with process experimentation under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) and Union Carbide. Conversely, once that molding process window is established and commercial production begins, running the press for 48 hours while automated vision scanners check for flash and QC technicians pull sample parts hourly to verify dimensional conformance against the blueprint is excluded quality control under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v).

In CNC Machining and First Article Inspection (FAI), a shop uses a Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) to measure the first part produced from a new CNC toolpath program against customer tolerances. If the initial machining run tests an unproven multi-axis fixturing and toolpath hypothesis for an exotic thin-walled alloy, and the FAI reveals tool deflection that forces the engineer to redesign the fixture, generate a "Rev 2" toolpath program, and machine a second experimental article to retest the hypothesis, that iterative loop functions as design/process reconfiguration under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7) and (a)(11) Example 4. Conversely, if the shop runs a proven CNC program and performs an FAI that immediately yields a "PASS" stamp confirming customer specifications, the FAI is a routine conformance check excluded under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and Little Sandy Coal.

In Metallurgy and Heat Treating, when a metallurgical lab tests multiple furnace atmosphere compositions, quench rates, and tempering temperatures on trial coupons and performs Rockwell hardness tests to determine which thermal profile eliminates cracking, the trials align with systematic trial-and-error experimentation (analogous to the shredding-blade material trials in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8), Example 3). By contrast, performing a Rockwell hardness check on an incoming shipment of commercial 4140 steel bar stock to verify that the vendor's delivery matches mill specifications is excluded incoming raw-material quality control under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and IRS Publication 5931.
Software Quality Assurance, Internal Use Software, and Beta Testing

In the software sector, the IRS Audit Guidelines on the Application of the Process of Experimentation for All Software specifically identify "Quality assurance (QA)/Testing (module, systems, integration, alpha, beta, performance, stress, regression, user acceptance, and manual testing, etc.)" as a critical audit review area, warning that activities categorized as "High risk" usually fail to constitute qualified research under IRC § 41(d).

Applying 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), the IRS Software Audit Guidelines, and Suder v. Commissioner, software testing divides into two distinct legal categories. Potentially qualified software experimentation encompasses architectural load, stress, and concurrency testing conducted during development to locate performance bottlenecks or race conditions where system architecture or data-caching synchronization is uncertain and failures drive code refactoring (as illustrated in the 2016 Treasury Preamble's data-caching and synchronization example under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8)), as well as iterative machine-learning (ML) validation that drives hyperparameter tuning and algorithmic redesign. Conversely, excluded software quality assurance encompasses routine regression testing of stable builds to confirm that updates did not break existing functionality, User Acceptance Testing (UAT) conducted by business users to verify workflow or cosmetic interface preferences (excluded under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and § 41(d)(4)(A)), and manual pass/fail QA test execution or administrative bug logging divorced from iterative code-level engineering.

When software is developed for internal corporate use rather than commercial sale, lease, or license, testing activities face an additional statutory hurdle under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(E) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6) governing Internal Use Software (IUS). Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(A)–(B), software is presumed to be developed primarily for internal use if it is developed for use in general and administrative (G&A) functions that facilitate or support the conduct of the taxpayer's trade or business—specifically defined across three exhaustive categories: (1) Financial management functions (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(1)), including accounts payable, accounts receivable, inventory management, budgeting, cash management, cost accounting, disbursements, economic analysis and forecasting, financial reporting, finance, fixed asset accounting, general ledger bookkeeping, internal audit, management accounting, risk management, strategic business planning, and tax (illustrated by employee health-benefit self-insurance reserve software in § 1.41-4(c)(6), Example 2); (2) Human resources management functions (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(2)), including recruiting, hiring, training, assigning personnel, and maintaining personnel records, payroll, and benefits (illustrated by an internet payroll self-service module in § 1.41-4(c)(6), Example 3); and (3) Support services (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)(3)), including data processing, facility services (grounds keeping, housekeeping, janitorial, and logistics), graphic services, marketing, legal services, government compliance services, printing and publication services, and security services.

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii), (iv), and (vi), software is exempted from IUS treatment if it is developed for commercial sale, lease, license, or marketing to third parties, or developed to enable the taxpayer to interact with third parties or allow third parties to initiate functions or review data on the taxpayer's system without supporting G&A functions (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(iv)), or if it is developed for use in an activity that constitutes qualified research (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(A)), developed for internal use in a qualified production process (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(B)), or developed together with hardware as a single integrated product used directly in providing services (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(C), Example 1). For dual function software (developed both for G&A functions and to enable third-party interaction under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vi)), the taxpayer may identify a discrete third-party subset ((c)(6)(vi)(B)) that is not subject to IUS rules, and for any remaining dual-function subset may elect a 25% safe harbor ((c)(6)(vi)(C)) if third-party interaction is reasonably anticipated to constitute at least 10% of the software's use and the research otherwise satisfies Section 41(d).

If software is classified as IUS (or is a remaining dual-function subset not using the 25% safe harbor), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)–(D) mandates that research and testing activities qualify only if, in addition to satisfying the standard four-part test of IRC § 41(d), the taxpayer establishes all three prongs of the High Threshold of Innovation Test at the beginning of software development:

items: Innovative (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(1), (B)): The software would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable improvement that is substantial and economically significant if the development is or would have been successful (a measurable objective standard rather than a determination of uniqueness or novelty).

Significant Economic Risk (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(2), (C)): The taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is "substantial uncertainty," because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period. 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C) explicitly states: "The term 'substantial uncertainty' requires a higher level of uncertainty and technical risk than that required for business components that are not internal use software."

Not Commercially Available (26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(A)(3)): The software cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

body.text: Applying this regulatory standard to an illustrative internal warehouse software comparison: if a company develops an internal logistics system (a G&A support/inventory function under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)(B)) and conducts stress testing on a custom distributed-ledger synchronization engine designed to synchronize inventory across 50 warehouses with zero latency where off-the-shelf software cannot handle the concurrency, that testing can qualify only if the project clears both the four-part test and the heightened "substantial uncertainty" and measurable improvement standards of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii). Conversely, testing the same warehouse system's user interface to confirm that clicking a "Print Label" button sends a formatted document to a printer is routine functional QA excluded under both 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v) and the IUS threshold.

Finally, for Beta Testing, the legal standard synthesized from Suder v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2014-201), the IRS Software Audit Guidelines, and 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) depends on whether the product has achieved commercial readiness and how beta feedback is utilized. When prototype units or pre-release builds are deployed to a targeted group of external beta testers while design uncertainties remain, and engineers actively use beta telemetry and bug reports to fix bugs and redesign hardware or software, the ongoing engineering bug-fixing loop qualifies as part of the process of experimentation under Suder. Conversely, releasing a commercially ready product as a "marketing beta" triggers disqualification under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), market testing under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(iii), and routine quality control under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v).

body.text: In the first scenario, the Hypothetical Biotech Polymer Stress Test vs. Batch Uniformity Check, a medical device manufacturer fabricates 50 biodegradable polymer heart-stent variations and subjects them to extreme thermal and mechanical stress testing until failure in order to discover a chemical formulation that maintains structural integrity, and subsequently pulls every 100th finished stent from an active commercial factory line to verify a fixed 2 mm thickness. Under federal tax law, fabricating and destructively testing the 50 prototype stent variations aligns with qualified pilot-model production and design-appropriateness testing under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4), (a)(7), and (a)(11) Example 5 (Multiple pilot models), and per Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287), both the pilot-model fabrication wages and the destructive laboratory testing costs enter the 80% experimentation numerator. Conversely, pulling every 100th commercial stent from the active factory line to confirm a 2 mm wall thickness is excluded both as post-commercial-production activity under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i) and as ordinary quality control inspection to verify conformance with specified parameters under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i), (a)(7), and § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v).

In the second scenario, the Hypothetical AeroTech Dynamics Composite Turbine Blade project, an aerospace manufacturer progresses through three phases: (A) molding 10 composite prototype blades with varying carbon-fiber/resin ratios and spin-testing them at 150% of operating speed until 8 of the 10 blades delaminate; (B) X-raying a 50-blade pilot production run to evaluate autoclave curing consistency; and (C) X-raying every 100th commercial production blade for internal voids and destructively testing commercial lot samples. Phase A qualifies as systematic trial-and-error experimentation on pilot models under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8) Example 3 and § 1.174-2(a)(4), making the engineering wages and destroyed prototype blade supplies eligible QREs under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)–(ii). Phase B is barred as product research under the "trial production runs" exclusion of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii)(C), and can qualify only if the autoclave manufacturing process separately satisfies Section 41(d) as an uncertain process business component under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), and Union Carbide (T.C. Memo. 2009-50)—provided further that under the Second Circuit's holding in Union Carbide (697 F.3d 104), the raw material costs of any pilot blades sold to customers are excluded from supply QREs. Phase C is 100% disqualified as post-production quality control inspection under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A), 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i), and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(10) Example 1, and commercial inventory blades destroyed in routine lot sampling do not qualify as research supplies.

In the third scenario, the Hypothetical LogisticsCorp ERP Migration project, an enterprise undertakes three software streams: (1) rewriting corrupted data-translation scripts to migrate 20 years of legacy data into a new ERP system; (2) re-architecting an API load balancer after simulated 50-robot concurrency tests cause system crashes; and (3) conducting Finance department User Acceptance Testing (UAT) to verify invoice printing and font sizes. Because an ERP and warehouse inventory system serves general and administrative financial and logistics support functions, it is subject to the Internal Use Software (IUS) rules of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii) unless exempted as a production process under § 1.41-4(c)(6)(ii)(B). Finance UAT checking invoice printing and font sizes is disqualified as routine quality control under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v), High Risk non-qualifying QA under the IRS Software Audit Guidelines, and cosmetic design testing under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B). Legacy data migration scripts face strict scrutiny under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5)(iv) (routine data collections) and the 2016 Treasury Preamble caveat that "routine programming" and standard debugging do not satisfy the process-of-experimentation or IUS High Threshold of Innovation tests. Conversely, by applying the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) to isolate the 50-robot concurrency load-balancer and caching re-architecture (paralleling the qualified data-caching and synchronization example in the 2016 Treasury Preamble to 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(8)), Workstream 2 can qualify if LogisticsCorp establishes either the production-process exemption or all three prongs of the High Threshold of Innovation test under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii).
Substantiation, Shrink-Back Methodology, and Compliance Analysis
Contemporaneous Documentation and Nexus Requirements

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(d) (Recordkeeping for the research credit), the Treasury Regulations mandate: "A taxpayer claiming a credit under section 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. For the rules governing record retention, see section 1.6001-1."

While the regulation does not prescribe a rigid list of mandatory documents, post-Little Sandy Coal jurisprudence has tightened judicial enforcement of the nexus between claimed expenditures and specific experimental testing activities. Although the Tax Court in Suder v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2014-201) credited executive testimony and retrospective allocation spreadsheets where ESI's ISO-9000 product development process was backed by 170,000 pages of exhibits (including bug reports, release notes, and schematics), the Seventh Circuit in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner (62 F.4th 287, 2023) and the Tax Court in Betz v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2023-84) rejected uncorroborated post-hoc estimates and generalized novelty assertions when experimental testing and routine production or quality control overlapped.

Most recently, in George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10 (summarized in a February 17, 2026 Grant Thornton tax alert), the U.S. Tax Court reinforced the decisive importance of contemporaneous trial records. In George, the sole shareholder of George's of Missouri, Inc. (GOMI)—an S corporation affiliate of the largest vertically integrated chicken producer in the United States—claimed pass-through research credits via amended returns for tax years 2012, 2013, and 2014 across seven agricultural research trials aimed at reducing broiler-chicken health issues, claiming solely supply QREs. Evaluating each trial individually under the four-part test and the "substantially all" requirement, the Tax Court held that four of the seven research trials constituted qualified research (in whole or in part) because the taxpayer adequately substantiated them through credible witness testimony and contemporaneous documentation. However, the court disallowed the remaining three trials due to poor-quality contemporaneous documentation that failed to establish project timelines, failed to identify which flocks were research flocks, failed to document the specific investigative activities performed (such as changes in drug dosage), or conflicted with witness testimony. (Notably, George also held that claiming supply QREs without claiming related wage QREs does not invalidate a research credit claim, and applied the statutory 6% credit rate calculation where base-period estimates lacked sufficient evidentiary documentation to apply the Cohan rule.)

Parallel to this judicial enforcement trend, the IRS has elevated business-component-level substantiation into an upfront return filing requirement through its overhaul of Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities). Following the release of a proposed draft Form 6765 on June 21, 2024, the publication of Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. January 2025), a June 18, 2025 IRS clarification regarding controlled-group member QRE reporting on Lines 5 and 20, and IRS News Release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS published finalized Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025, posted February 6, 2026), superseding the January 2025 revision.

Under the finalized December 2025 Form 6765 instructions and IR-2025-99, completing new Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before 2026 (including tax year 2025), and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (tax year 2026 and beyond), subject to exemptions for Qualified Small Business (QSB) taxpayers electing the payroll tax research credit (up to the $500,000 cap on Section D) and taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less. Filers required to complete Section G must follow the "80%/Top 50" business components rule, reporting detailed component-by-component information for a minimum of 80% of total QREs or a maximum of 50 business components, and reporting any remaining components in aggregate by entering "Aggregate Business Components" in column 49(c). For each reported component, the filer must classify the component type in column 49(d) (Product, Process, or All Others), identify software categories in line 49(e) if applicable (A. IUS, B. DFS [Dual Function Software], or C. Excepted from IUS treatment), and report itemized expenditures across Column 50 (in-house wages for direct conduct of qualified research), Column 51 (in-house wages for direct supervision / first-line management), Column 52 (in-house wages for direct support, such as a laboratory worker cleaning equipment or a clerk compiling research data, excluding general administrative services), Column 53 (total qualified wages), Column 54 (supplies), Column 55 (off-premises computer rental/lease), and Column 56 (contract research expenses). In addition, Item A at the top of Form 6765 requires taxpayers to make their timely IRC § 280C election (choosing either the reduced credit rate of 15.8% on Line 13 instead of the 20% regular credit rate, or reducing their Section 174A domestic R&E deduction/capitalized expenses and attaching statement Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf).
Shrink-Back Analysis and Hypothetical Worked Calculation

When excluded quality control testing, standard assembly integration, or commercial readiness checks cause a top-level product (such as an entire vessel, vehicle, or enterprise software system) to fall below the 80% "substantially all" threshold of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the taxpayer's primary regulatory mechanism to preserve credit eligibility is the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) (paired with the Section 174 component rule in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5)).

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2), if the requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2) are not satisfied at the level of the overall product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention, those requirements are applied to the most significant subset of elements of the business component: "This shrinking back of the product is to continue until either a subset of elements of the product that satisfies the requirements is reached, or the most basic element of the product is reached and such element fails to satisfy the test. This shrinking-back rule is applied only if a taxpayer does not satisfy the requirements of section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a)(2) of this section with respect to the overall business component. The shrinking-back rule is not itself applied as a reason to exclude research activities from credit eligibility." In the accompanying illustration in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(3), Example, motorcycle engine builder X develops a new carburetor and modifies an existing engine design for use with the new carburetor; if the modifications to the engine viewed as a whole fail the requirements of Section 41(d)(1) and paragraph (a), the requirements are applied to the next most significant subset of elements—the carburetor—whose development may constitute qualified research.

Adapting an illustrative "New Car" and "New Fuel Injection System" (95% experimental) scenario using statutory rates and thresholds—the 80% "substantially all" threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the 100% inclusion rate for in-house wages and supplies under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), the 65% inclusion cap for third-party contract research under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A), the 20% regular credit rate under 26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1), and the 15.8% reduced credit rate under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c) and Form 6765 Line 13—the following Hypothetical worked calculation demonstrates the exact mathematical and compliance mechanics of segregating quality control testing via the shrinking-back rule.

In Step 1 (Whole-Vehicle Evaluation), assume a domestic automotive manufacturer incurs $1,000,000 in total development, integration, and testing expenses on a "New Car" project, of which $190,000 involves iterative prototype testing and redesign of a novel New Fuel Injection System to resolve technical uncertainty, and $810,000 consists of routine chassis assembly checks, compliance verification, and quality control inspections against established specifications ($190,000 + $810,000 = $1,000,000). Dividing $190,000 of experimental activities by $1,000,000 of total vehicle activities yields an experimentation ratio of 19.0%, which falls well below the 80.0% "substantially all" threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). Claimed on an indivisible whole-vehicle basis without subcomponent cost records—as occurred in Trinity Industries (on the T-AGS 60 and XFPB) and Little Sandy Coal—the entire $1,000,000 claim fails and $0 qualifies for the credit.

In Step 2 (Proactive Shrink-Back to the Fuel Injection Subsystem), applying 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) and (b)(3), the taxpayer shrinks back the business component from the overall vehicle to the discrete New Fuel Injection System subcomponent. Contemporaneous project accounting isolates a $200,000 total activity pool for the Fuel Injection System, comprising $190,000 in iterative hypothesis testing, pilot-model injector fabrication, and design retesting, plus $10,000 in non-experimental dimensional quality control inspection of finished injector nozzles ($190,000 + $10,000 = $200,000). Dividing $190,000 by $200,000 yields an experimentation ratio of 95.0%, satisfying the 80.0% "substantially all" threshold of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6). However, as clarified in 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6) and T.D. 8930, satisfying the 80% threshold for the subcomponent does not render the remaining 5% ($10,000) of routine quality control inspection credit-eligible; the $10,000 of ordinary quality control inspection remains excluded from QREs under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v).

In Step 3 (QRE and Tentative Credit Computation), assume the $190,000 of qualified experimental activity on the New Fuel Injection System consists of $110,000 in qualifying domestic in-house engineering wages (100% eligible under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(i) and § 174A, reported in Form 6765 Section G, Columns 50–53), $30,000 in destroyed prototype injector supplies (100% eligible under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), reported in Column 54), and $50,000 paid to an external domestic laboratory for destructive prototype testing (65% eligible under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A), yielding $50,000 × 65% = $32,500 in contract research QREs reported in Column 56). Summing $110,000 in wages, $30,000 in supplies, and $32,500 in contract research yields $172,500 in total QREs. Strategic Compliance Recommendations

items: Conduct a Testing Inventory Audit: Map all QA, QC, laboratory, and validation roles against federal tax rules by evaluating test-failure outcomes—if a failed test leads to scrap or rework of a unit, the activity points toward excluded quality control (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i); § 1.41-4(c)(5)(v)), whereas if a failure triggers engineering reconfiguration and design retesting to resolve an inappropriate design, it points toward potentially qualified research (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(7) and (a)(11) Example 4).

Implement Phase-Gate Terminology and Timeline Mapping: Define a formal "Design Transfer" or "Commercial Production Release" gate (aligned with the "product release" sign-offs noted in the IRS Audit Techniques Guide under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i)), relabeling misnamed "QC" prototype destruction tests as "Design Validation" only where contemporaneous engineering records verify unresolved design uncertainty.

Refine Hybrid Time-Tracking Codes: Establish separate time-tracking codes for dual-role engineers and technicians (such as "New Product Development / Subcomponent Experimentation" versus "Routine Testing / Calibration / Production Support") to provide the principled allocation demanded by Little Sandy Coal (62 F.4th 287) and populate Columns 50, 51, and 52 of Form 6765 Section G.

Maintain a Failed-Test Repository: Preserve pre-test protocols stating technical hypotheses, crash logs, broken prototypes, and engineering ticket threads documenting root-cause analysis (rather than bare administrative entries such as "Fix Bug #102") to substantiate the scientific method required under Union Carbide, Suder, Little Sandy Coal, and George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10).

Apply Shrink-Back Proactively and Consult Tax Counsel: Segregate experimental subsystems prior to filing under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) and § 1.174-2(a)(5) to preserve the 80% threshold and satisfy Form 6765 Section G's 80%/Top 50 business component reporting rules, and engage qualified tax counsel to evaluate testing methodologies under current IRC Section 174A, Section 280C, and Section 41 standards.
